pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — What Is the Ocean? (ages 5–7): the ocean is a huge body of SALT water that covers most of Earth's surface (about 71% — more sea than land) and is home to an enormous number of living things.
• Standards — UK (DfE): supports KS1 Y1/Y2 'Animals, including humans' and 'Living things and their habitats' (habitats provide for living things), and links to geography KS1 (name/locate seas and oceans); an early awareness-and-wonder foundation.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 relevance (organisms and the places they live); 2-LS4-1 (there are many kinds of living things in different places) — the ocean as the largest such place.
• Operational details: establish three concrete ideas — (1) the ocean is SALTY, unlike the fresh water children drink, swim in at a pool, or see in rivers/lakes; (2) there is MORE ocean than land on Earth (a blue planet); (3) it is FULL of life, more than anywhere else. Use a globe/world map so 'covers most of Earth' is seen, and a taste-memory hook (seawater is salty, you can't drink it). Keep quantities qualitative ('most', 'huge') at this age.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~5–6): say the ocean is huge, salty water with lots of animals in it. B (transitional, ~6–7): state there is more ocean than land on Earth and that ocean water is salty, unlike river/lake water. C (early formal, ~7): explain the ocean covers most of Earth's surface and is home to more living things than land.
bestPractices: Use a globe or blue-marble image so 'covers most of Earth' is a seen fact (more blue than green), not a told one.
Anchor 'salty' to sensory memory — seawater tastes salty and can't be drunk — and contrast with the fresh water of taps, rivers and lakes so salt vs fresh is concrete.
Lead with wonder and variety (the ocean is stuffed with living things) to motivate the whole domain, not just facts about water.
Distinguish 'sea/ocean' from other water children know (puddles, pools, ponds, rivers) by size and saltiness.
keyRepresentations: A globe/world map with ocean vs land clearly contrasted (blue dominating green).
A salt-vs-fresh water pairing (sea beside a river/tap) with a 'don't drink me' salt cue.
A cutaway 'peek beneath the surface' teeming with varied sea life.
A simple size comparison: how much of Earth is ocean vs land.
commonMisconceptions: 'There's more land than sea' — the ocean covers most of Earth (about 71%).
'Ocean water is like the water we drink' — it is salty and unsafe to drink, unlike fresh river/lake/tap water.
'The sea is just a big puddle / empty water' — it is vast, deep, and full of more life than land.
'Seas and oceans are totally separate pools' — the ocean is really one connected body of water around the world.
'Only fish live in the ocean' — mammals, invertebrates, plants/algae and countless others live there too.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, build awareness and wonder that the ocean is a huge body of salty water covering most of Earth's surface and home to an enormous variety of living things. Core moves: let children SEE on a globe/world map that there is more blue (ocean) than green (land); anchor 'salty' to sensory memory and contrast with the fresh water of taps, rivers and lakes; and reveal the teeming life beneath the surface. Keep quantities qualitative ('most', 'huge') at this age.

activities.title: Meet the ocean: globe reveal, salt flap, and dive-in
feedback: When the child notices more blue than green: 'You spotted it yourself — Earth has more sea than land. That's why it's sometimes called the blue planet.'

On the salt flap: 'Sea water is salty, so we can't drink it even when we're thirsty. River and tap water are fresh, not salty. Tap water has been cleaned so it is safe to drink, but river water needs cleaning before anyone drinks it.'
When the underwater scene opens: 'Look how many different animals live here! So many kinds of creatures live in the ocean — big ones, tiny ones, and all sorts of shapes.'
activities.rationale: A seen fact (blue dominating green on a map) lands the 'covers most of Earth' idea as something the child noticed rather than was told. A sensory salt anchor and a fresh-water contrast make salt vs fresh concrete. Leading with the variety of sea life motivates the whole domain at an awareness level appropriate for 5–7.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
Living things live in habitats that provide for their needs; there are many kinds of living things in different places — the ocean being the largest.
learnerActions: Look at a globe or world map and point to the blue parts (water) and the land parts (often green or brown — check the map's colours); say out loud which there is more of.
Lift a flap or reveal panel on the water to meet the question 'Why can't you drink it?' and hear the salt fact, with a river or tap pictured alongside for contrast.

'Dive in' beneath the waves (turn a page, open an underwater scene, or tap a drill-down panel) to discover a world packed with creatures of many shapes and sizes — whales, fish, crabs, jellyfish, seahorses.
activities.intendedInsight: Our planet's surface is mostly ocean; ocean water is salty (unlike the fresh water we drink); and the ocean is home to a huge variety of living things.

activities.title: Paint the globe / sort the water (hands-on scaffold)
feedback: After painting: 'Which colour covered the most? Blue — so there is more ocean than land.'
After sorting: 'The sea went in the salty group; the rivers, lakes and taps in our pictures are fresh water. Most lakes are fresh, though a few special lakes are salty.'
activities.rationale: A simple manipulable lets children feel the proportion and the salt/fresh split. At this age the concept is awareness-level, so this is an optional reinforcing activity rather than a required live model.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
learnerActions: Paint or place blue tiles over the water parts of a world outline and green over the land, then look at how much more blue there is.
Sort pictures or labels of water sources into two groups: salty (the sea/ocean) and fresh (river, lake, tap).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Most of Earth is ocean' and 'salty vs fresh' become felt through doing, not just seen.

activities.title: Talk it through: how is the ocean different from a lake?
feedback: Correct response: 'Ocean water is salty, while river and most lake water is fresh — the salt is why you can't drink sea water. And the ocean covers more of Earth than land does — most of the planet's surface.'
If the child says there's more land: show a globe and estimate blue vs green — most of it is blue; let the map overrule the land-dweller's hunch.
If the child says ocean water is fresh like a river: recall a seaside taste memory (salty, stings a cut) versus tap/river water, and name fresh vs salt. (No tasting of unknown water in class.)
If the child describes the ocean only as 'the beach we went to': zoom out on a globe — the ocean is one enormous connected body of salt water around most of the planet, not just one beach.
activities.rationale: Short spoken discussion surfaces the three common misconceptions (more land than ocean; ocean water is fresh; 'ocean' means one local beach) and lets responsive feedback address each. The two independent facts (salty; covers-more) separate genuine understanding from everyday guessing.
sourceClaims: The ocean covers more than 70 percent (about 71%) of Earth's surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.
Ocean (salt) water differs from the fresh water of rivers, lakes and taps and is not safe to drink.
learnerActions: Respond to: 'A lake is big too. Name one thing that makes the OCEAN different from a big lake.' (Looking for salt and/or vast scale.)
Decide and explain: 'Is there just one ocean or lots of separate ones — what do you think?' then look at a globe to see the water is really one connected body wrapping the planet.

Answer the challenge: 'Someone says the ocean is just a really big lake, the water is the same as a river, and there's more land than ocean. Are they right? Tell me one way ocean water is different, and whether land or ocean covers more of Earth.'
activities.intendedInsight: The ocean is distinguished from familiar water (puddles, pools, ponds, rivers, lakes) by its saltiness and its vast, connected scale — and both facts can be held at once.

constraints: Keep quantities qualitative at this age ('most', 'huge'); do not require children to work with the precise 71% or 97% figures.
Safety: never have children taste unknown or sea water in class; rely on remembered seaside taste and pictured comparisons.

A couple of picture recognition questions (which is salty? more sea or land?) can check recall but do not by themselves elicit the child's own explanation; use them as a light check, not the main activity.

Painting the globe and sorting water sources are reinforcing scaffolds; the central aim is that the child notices and can state both facts and picture the ocean's life, not just complete a sorting task.
Address the connectedness idea (the ocean is really one body of water around the world) as part of 'what the ocean is', since children often picture separate pools.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original artefact notes claimed '3D adds no conceptual payoff' and that a scored quiz 'can't build the wonder'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been removed from learner-facing text and reframed as narrow scope limits (a quiz is a light recall check; a rotatable globe is an optional dramatisation).

One source (NGSS/DfE habitats claim) is marked verified:false in the row; the 'ocean is the largest such place' framing — and the derived 'more living things than on land' message — is attributed but not independently verified here. The original's stronger 'more than anywhere else on Earth' superlative has been narrowed to 'more than on land' in learner-facing text.

The original diagnostic feedback said 'about two-thirds' while NOAA cites about 71% (which exceeds two-thirds). Learner-facing feedback now uses the qualitative 'most'; the two-thirds/71% imprecision is recorded here only, not presented to children.
The 'only fish live in the ocean' misconception from the source is addressed implicitly via the varied-creatures reveal rather than named explicitly; could be made explicit if desired.

probeDeeper: 'Why can't you drink sea water when you're thirsty, but you can drink water from a tap?'
'Look at the globe — point to more blue or more green? So which is there more of, ocean or land?'
'A lake is big too. Name one thing that makes the OCEAN different from a big lake.' (salt + scale counterexample)
'Is there just one ocean or lots of separate ones — what do you think?'
assess.correctAnswer: They're not right on either count. Ocean water is SALTY, while river and lake water is fresh (not salty) — that's why you can't drink sea water. And the ocean covers MORE of the Earth than land does (about two-thirds / most of the planet's surface is ocean).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks there is more land than ocean on Earth ('we live on land, there's loads of it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a globe or world map and spin/estimate blue vs green — most of it is blue. Name it: about two-thirds ocean. Let the map overrule the land-dweller's intuition.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's more land than ocean on Earth
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says land covers more; surprised the ocean is the majority of the surface

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks ocean water is the same fresh water as a river or lake ('water is just water')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a taste memory (seaside — salty, stings a cut) with tap/river water. Name fresh vs salt; that's the key difference. (No tasting of unknown water in class.)
errorPatterns.distractor: The ocean is fresh water, the same as a river
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the ocean is salty, or says you could drink sea water like river water

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks 'the ocean' is one particular place they've visited (a beach) rather than a huge body of water covering most of Earth
errorPatterns.nextMove: Zoom out on a globe: the ocean is one enormous connected body of salt water wrapping most of the planet, not just one beach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the ocean only as 'the beach we went to'; no sense of its vast global scale

responseLevels.gap: Says there's more land than ocean, or that ocean water is fresh like a river; treats 'ocean' as just a local beach.
responseLevels.full: States the ocean is salt water (unlike fresh rivers/lakes) AND that it covers more of Earth than land, and can picture it as one huge body of water home to countless living things — connecting the facts rather than reciting one.
responseLevels.partial: Gets one fact (salty OR covers-more) but not both, or states them as memorised words without conviction — e.g. says 'salty' but thinks land covers more.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says: 'The ocean is just a really big lake — the water is the same as the water in a river, and there's more land on Earth than ocean anyway.' Are they right? Tell me one way ocean water is different from river water, and whether land or ocean covers more of the Earth.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who knows what the ocean is says salt water (not fresh) AND that ocean covers more than land. A child guessing from everyday experience — we live on land, maps show lots of countries — says there's more land, or that 'water is just water' with no salt/fresh distinction. The two tiers separate the two independent facts; getting both right can't easily happen by luck.
